title: Chapter 19 – Columns of Numbers
html:
Grandfather listens to the whole story without moving.

He sits in his plain chair at the end of the council table with the dawn behind him, and Lin Jian stands before him with his hands at his sides and tells it the way Feng advised: exactly what he saw, and not one word of what he did. The cliff. The pink trail. The ice door that opened for a boy who stood still. The red lamp, the spiral, the dying man in the middle of it. The lamp chain snapping, and the fire.

"It fell on its own," Grandfather says.

"The chain was old, Grandfather. Bone and iron rot in blood. It was holding by one link."

"And the pin in the stone?"

Lin Jian keeps his face still. "Hu's pins are the best in the valley. I thought if I could jam the basin, it might stop mending him. I drove one in, and the basin turned."

It is a half-truth wrapped around a whole one, and the old man looks at him for a long time. Then he nods once, as if closing a ledger. "You will tell it exactly that way to everyone. The basin turned on him. The lamp fell. A man bleeding pepper from six holes and a Lin knife in his ribs died in his own den." He lifts a hand. "And that is all that anyone in this valley will ever hear."

"What do we do with the cave?"

"Feng's men are stripping it now. Everything portable, down to the lamp bowl. The basin we will break." Grandfather's mouth tightens. "I will not leave a Blood Shadow formation standing on my mountain for some herb-gatherer to wander into."

That is how the Hollow learns, by noon, that the Crimson Vulture is dead. The story runs through the terraces faster than the guards can carry it: a demonic cultivator, wounded in the north by Lin warriors, crawled into a cave to die and was found by Lin guards at dawn. Nobody mentions a boy. The gates stand open for the first time in forty days. The villagers who sheltered inside the walls go home carrying their bedrolls, and in the evening the hall doors are propped wide, and the whole family eats with the sound of children and goats drifting in from the yard.

Lin Jian eats very little. He is thinking about a gray hand on his ankle.

* * *

He studies it that night by the light of a Clear Light chip, in the room he shares with nobody.

The band has not faded. It has not spread either. It is a hand-shaped bruise the color of wet slate, four fingers and a thumb, with a faint grain in it like the grain of old wood. He pulls up his leg wrap and puts two fingers against it, and the skin is dry and slightly cool, but he feels the pulse beneath it. Whatever it is, it is still part of him.

Scan.

```
[Scan — Left Ankle, Band]
Tissue: dermal + subdermal, Qi-saturated
Foreign element: blood-lattice (Blood Shadow type), 3.1% active
Behavior: inert; no spread observed in 14 h
Source: Blood-Spiral Basin, relay contact
Recommended: do not Separate (living tissue — LOCKED at Level 2)
Estimated risk if left: unknown
```

Three percent. A lattice, a mesh of threads running through his skin, like the veins of a leaf. He thinks of the way the basin pulled at his legs when he waded the channel, and the way it did not pull hard. It is deciding whose blood it wants. It has marked him as a maybe.

Unknown risk. That is not an answer. That is a debt.

He rolls the leg wrap down, and wraps the ankle in a strip of linen, and tells himself that when he reaches Level 3 he will deal with it. It is the second thing on a list that grows longer every week.

* * *

Old Hu sits up on the third day.

He is gray and thin and he complains about the porridge, which Lin Jian takes as the best sign yet. His wound has closed to a pink seam, and the black thread that had crept through it like a hair in milk has gone. Su Qinghe sits by his bed with a bowl in her lap, watching him eat the way a hawk watches a field.

"Strained poultice," Hu says, around a mouthful. "Cleaned my own blood out of a healer's bandage. The boy's mother tells me you sat up with me all night, radish."

"Yes."

"Why?"

"Because the cut was feeding the residue, and the poultice was feeding the cut."

"Hm." Hu chews. His eye goes to the bundle on the table by the window, a long shape wrapped in the dead man's black veil. Feng has carried it up from the cave himself, handling it as though it were a snake. "And that?"

Lin Jian unwraps it.

The curved blade lies on the cloth like a bone. In daylight it is paler, and not as ugly as it was in the cave. It is a good weapon. Lin Jian knows that the way he knows his own handwriting: the line of the spine is perfect, the grain of the steel is tight and even, and the edge, even dulled by blood, still holds a thin shining thread of light.

Hu does not touch it. He looks at it, and then at the tang, and at the small stamp where the wrapping has slid.

A hammer and a wave.

"That's mine," he says.

Nobody speaks.

"Twenty years ago," Hu says. His voice is level, but the hand holding the spoon has begun to shake. "I forged a blade for the Veiled Forge, the Sect's own refiners. A Profound-grade weapon, a hundred and nine folds of spirit iron over a bone core. They said it was for an elder named Sha, and the blade took his name. I thought it was the best thing I would ever make." He puts the spoon down. "Then they quenched it."

"In what?" says Su Qinghe softly.

"In blood. Not any blood. The elder's. Drawn over three days, from a man who had refined his own blood for a century." Hu's one eye closes. "I stood there and watched them drop it in. I heard it scream. I do not think I have ever heard anything scream like that, before or since. I ran that night, and Sha caught me at the gate and took my arm at the shoulder. With that." He nods at the bundle. "The elder is dead now. His pupil carried it, and it cut me a second time two weeks ago, in a pit under the cedars. It remembers me."

Lin Jian thinks of the way the residue in the old man's wound reached for the blade across a cedar clearing. The blade is calling it. He thought he was being poetic.

"What will you do with it?" Su Qinghe says.

"Melt it down," says Hu. He opens his eye. "If I can."

"If you can?"

"It is worth more than the pouch." A flat smile. "A mid-grade spirit weapon is worth a hundred stones to anyone with sense. And I am a refiner, Qinghe. I have never in my life melted down a thing I made well." He is quiet for a moment. "Give me a month. I will think about what it wants to be."

* * *

Lin Wenshi, who commands the gate guards, brings the report on the cave to the council: forty-one items, Feng's lists in a neat hand. The basin is broken. The lamp bowl has been carried to the forge. The leather pouch on the dead man's chest held six low-grade spirit stones, as Lin Jian said. But in a niche behind the pillar, a hand's depth in the wall, Feng's men found a lacquered box with a Sect stamp on the lid, and in the box a hundred and eighteen stones, wrapped in oiled cloth.

"The Sect pays its assassins in advance," Grandfather says. "And keeps the change in the wall." He puts one finger on the lid of the box. "This is the first thing that has come out of Blood Shadow's hands in forty days that is of any use to us."

The treasury is a plain stone room behind the council hall, with a brass lock that has not been changed in forty years. The box goes in. Nobody says aloud what it will be used for, but nobody needs to. A hundred and eighteen low-grade stones is a little more than the price of the cheapest Foundation Establishment pill on the Willow Ford market.

Across the table, Second Uncle sits with his hands folded and his eyes on the grain of the wood. When the number is read, he lets out a long, slow breath through his nose. His fingers go to the left side of his neck and press there, quickly, and drop.

It is not a large gesture. Lin Jian would not have seen it a year ago. But a year ago he could not see the faint, wavering color of a man's Qi, and Wenhai's color, which has been for months a tight, strained, clenched thing, like a fist around a rope, has just opened. The knot has gone out of it.

Something was tied to his neck, and it is gone.

He does not know what. A seed, a leash, a promise sealed in blood. All he knows is that the man who sat under it for weeks is lighter today than he was yesterday, and that the only thing that has changed is that Gu Yan is dead. Beneath the table, where nobody can see, Lin Jian's hand closes on his knee.

He is relieved. He did not want the Vulture to come back, and he did not want it dead enough to say so.

It is an interesting thought. He files it with the others.

* * *

The arbiter is twelve days away.

Grandfather says so at the end of the council, in a quiet voice, with the doors closed. The Zhao petition goes to the arbiter's table on the first dry morning of spring: the spring, and the channel cut from it, claimed by a survey a hundred and forty years old. If the Lins cannot show a deed, they lose the water that feeds half their terraces. If they lose that, they lose the harvest, and the Hollow is back where it began, on its knees.

"There is a deed," Grandfather says. "There has always been a deed. Lin Shoucheng registered it in his own lifetime." He looks, for the first time in Lin Jian's memory, tired. "It lay in a lacquered tube on the second shelf of the library for a hundred and fifty years. Since the storm, it has not lain anywhere."

Nobody looks at Wenhai. It is the most deliberate silence Lin Jian has ever heard.

"I have searched the library every night since the roof fell," Grandfather says. "I have not found it. I do not expect to." He folds his hands. "Which means that when the arbiter asks for the deed, we will have nothing to say. Unless someone has something to say about why."

He lets the room think about that. Then he adjourns the council, and the room empties, and Wenhai is the last man to leave.

* * *

"Everybody skims," says Lin Jian's father.

It is the afternoon of the second day after, and they are walking to Willow Ford on a damp, bright road with the first green showing on the willows. Father carries a satchel of talismans on his shoulder. Mother walks on the other side, with a basket and a quiet face. She is dressed as a farmer's wife. The disguise is perfect, and she is utterly unmistakable.

"Everybody skims," Father says again, patiently, as though he is reciting a catechism. "It is what a steward is for. A shop that makes a profit can bear a little loss, and everyone knows it. Grandfather knew it before you were born." He smiles at his son. "That is why we do not take every discrepancy to the council."

"How much do they skim?"

"A little. A fifth, perhaps. In bad years, a third."

"And what would Wenhai have to take," Lin Jian says, "to make the shop's books look like a loss when the shop sells every talisman you draw?"

His father opens his mouth. Closes it.

The road bends. The willows thin out. And ahead, over a low rise, the roofs of Willow Ford appear.

It is the biggest place Lin Jian has ever seen with his own eyes. Three thousand people live here, in long gray rows of timber and tile and rammed earth, on both banks of a wide brown river joined by a wooden bridge as old as the Hollow. The east wall is real stone, with a gate and a pair of Sect banners. The market square lies in the middle of the town like a fist in a glove. And in it, in the thin spring sunlight, a thousand ordinary people are using spells.

The first time, at six, the details slid past him. Now he looks properly. A baker's boy flicks a Heat Plate from a stack of yellow slips into his oven and takes off the lid to find the loaves already done. A woman scrubbing a stoop slaps a green Dust-Away on the stone and watches the grime lift off in a gray skin, curling like an orange peel. At the well, an old man in a straw hat fills a bucket and sets a Clear Water slip against its rim, and the cloudy river water goes silver and sweet. A girl runs past with a Spirit Lantern on a stick: not a candle, just a coin-sized crystal, humming with warm gold light. Overhead, a flock of sparrows scatters from a rooftop where a sign painter has slapped a Wind-Ward on a pole, a talisman that sheds birds, rain and leaves.

These are not grand things. They are the small Qi-work of a world that has lived with cultivation for ten thousand years: the cleaning, the heat, the water, the light. Nobody notices them. They are as ordinary as soap.

And on the north side of the square, across a dusty cobbled space from a very quiet building, stands the shop.

Green Pine Talismans and Herbs. The sign is a painted pine on a green board. The windows are wide and the door is open. Beyond it, a small, bald man in a black apron is shouting at someone about the price of rain slips.

Across the square, a larger and grander and almost empty shop, with a gilt sign and a bored clerk in the doorway, says Zhao Family Spirit Goods.

Father follows his gaze and smiles with one side of his mouth. "They sell to the Sect's officers and to people who like to be seen buying from them," he says. "We sell to everyone else."

"There are more of everyone else."

"There always are."

* * *

Old Fang sells talismans the way some men play a drum.

He is perhaps sixty-five, five feet nothing, bald as an egg, with a wisp of white beard and eyes like two wet black beads. He cannot read. He has never learned his letters. He has kept the Lin shop for thirty-one years without a ledger, and the Lin family have never asked him to keep one, because for thirty-one years he has done something better.

He keeps sticks.

In the back room, behind the counter, there are bundles of bamboo tally sticks hanging from the ceiling in colored cord: red for spring, yellow for summer, green for autumn, blue for winter. Each stick is the length of a forearm. Each is covered in notches. On the left side, one notch for every box of talismans received from the Hollow. On the right, one notch for every ten sold. At the end of every month, a clean cut across the middle, and the date scratched beside it in a sort of private code that only Old Fang can read.

"I like to know," he says, when Lin Jian asks. He says it as though it explains the universe. "A man who doesn't know what he's got is a man who's about to be robbed. I don't need to read. I need to count."

Lin Jian looks at the sticks, and a very quiet thing happens in his chest.

There they are.

"May I see the winter set, Old Fang? From the year before last."

The old man regards him for a moment. Then he reaches up without looking and takes down a bundle of four blue sticks, bound at the top with a knot Lin Jian does not recognize, and puts it in the boy's hands.

He holds them as carefully as he has ever held anything.

```
[Scan — Tally Sticks, Winter Set]
Material: bamboo, 4 sticks, cut and notched by hand
Notch count: left 212, right 431
Tool: single knife, right-handed; consistent angle
Age of cuts: consistent with claimed dates; oxidation gradient matches
Alteration check: no re-cuts, no filled notches, no foreign tool marks
Authenticity: 99.1%
Cost: 2 CE
```

He hoped for it without being sure. This is the thing Second Uncle cannot fake, because Second Uncle has never seen it: a record that was not written for him. Every notch has an age. Every cut has a tool, a hand, a day. If Old Fang's sticks say a box of talismans arrived on a given morning, and if the sticks match the oxidation of the bamboo around each notch, then nobody in the world can say the box did not arrive.

He turns to his father. "Can Old Fang testify before the council?"

Father is staring at the sticks. He has not said a word since Lin Jian picked them up. There is a look on his face that Lin Jian has not seen in some time, and it takes him a moment to place it. It is the look of a man who has just learned what his own son is doing.

"Old Fang will testify," says Old Fang placidly, from the doorway. "If the old man wants."

"The old man?"

"Your grandfather." The wet black eyes twinkle. "He has been asking me about my sticks for ten years. I have been waiting for someone to come and look at them properly."

* * *

They leave Willow Ford at dusk, with four blue sticks wrapped in oilcloth in Lin Jian's satchel and a promise from Old Fang that every other bundle will be in the Hollow by the end of the week.

Father walks beside him the whole way home. It is a long road, and he says nothing for the first mile.

"The sticks," he says at last.

"Yes, Father."

"You knew about them."

"I heard Old Fang shouting prices at the autumn market. I wondered how he knew them." Lin Jian keeps his eyes on the road. "I thought a man who does not write must count."

"And the rest?"

"What rest?"

His father laughs, once, not unkindly. "Jian, I have drawn talismans for thirty years. I have a practice book. I write a line for every night since I was sixteen: the date, the talisman, how many I tried, how many held. I have never shown it to anyone." He glances over. "I found it open on my desk this morning, at the right place, with the page marked."

Lin Jian is silent.

"Twelve volumes," Father says. "Every night. I can tell you how many Fire Starters I drew in the second week of the ninth month eight years ago. I can tell you how many Flame-Bursts failed. If I know that, and Old Fang knows how many boxes he received, and Third Aunt's ledgers know how many herbs went to the shop..." He shakes his head slowly. "I think you have been very busy."

"I have always been very busy."

"I think," Father says, "that I am going to stop asking you questions I do not want answered, and start giving you the books."

It is the nicest thing anyone has said to Lin Jian all spring.

* * *

He needs six nights.

He does it in the barred granary, behind a door that Dong guards and a window that Kai has papered over, with a pot of tea, four blue sticks, forty-one pages of Father's practice book, and a lamp. Old Fang's other bundles arrive on the third night, all forty seasons of them, tied in colored cord. Third Aunt sends her herb ledgers. Grandfather himself brings a thin wooden box and sets it at the end of the table without a word: ten years of council minutes, in Wenhai's own hand.

It is the least romantic work he has ever done.

There are forty seasons. There are seven columns for each: boxes shipped, boxes received, talismans per box, sold per notch, price per notch, coin returned, coin reported. Forty seasons by seven columns, two hundred and eighty numbers, each of which must agree with its neighbors to within the sort of error a mortal can make. He does it twice, once in his head, once in ink. And then, on the fourth night, with the lamp low, he puts down the brush and looks at what he has made, and a very cold feeling settles in the back of his neck.

The numbers do not wobble.

A man who is skimming a little, a fifth, a third, leaves a mess. His reports lurch and breathe with the real flow of trade, because a smart thief steals in proportion, and a proportion is a thing that rises and falls. But the numbers in front of Lin Jian are perfectly flat. For thirty-six seasons, nine years, Wenhai's reported coin falls short of the real by eight or nine stones every season. Not two. Not twenty. Eight, nine, ten, nine, eight, a small flat line of theft, as regular as a pulse.

That is not skimming, he thinks. That is a salary.

And then, four seasons from the end, something changes.

The Hollander beater. The yellow paper. The talismans that sell for a quarter-stone each, and then half a stone, and then, in the winter after the Mirror Guard contract, three. The real money rises, and Wenhai's line rises with it. Forty-eight stones in the first season of the new paper. Fifty-one. Fifty-three. Forty-four in the winter, when the roads are closed.

He puts the brush down.

He does the sum a third time. Then he sits very still, and listens to the lamp hiss, and the grain-mice moving in the wall.

Five hundred and twelve low-grade spirit stones in ten years.

It is more than a village earns in a century. It is enough to buy a Foundation Establishment pill, and a good teacher, and a second chance for a clan that has never had one. It is the whole of the thing the Lin family has been missing: the difference between a hill that starves and a hill that eats. And it has gone through one man's hands, quietly and regularly, in the shape of a steward's small kindnesses, for as long as Lin Jian has been alive.

Under the sum, in the margin, he writes a single line.

This is not for the council. This is for the arbiter. The council needs a verdict. The arbiter needs a number.

He blows out the lamp.

* * *

His mother is waiting in the yard.

She does not say anything. She holds out her hand, and he places the sheet in it: forty seasons, seven columns, the total at the foot in his small clear hand. She reads it standing under the stars, once, with the lamp-glow from the kitchen window on her face. Her lips move very slightly at the bottom.

"Five hundred and twelve," she says.

"Yes, Mother."

"How certain are you?"

"The smallest numbers the evidence allows. The real figure is higher."

She folds the sheet. It goes into the sleeve of her short robe, the place where she keeps knives. "This is enough to take to the council," she says. There is no triumph in it. Her voice is perfectly flat. "It is enough to break him, even before the arbiter."

"But?"

"But the arbiter is in four days, and the council will take longer, and the spring is first." She looks at him. "Your grandfather will not hang a man for what he stole from the Lins while the Zhao are at the door to steal the rest. First the channel. Then Wenhai."

"And the deed?"

"Is gone." Mother's eyes are very dark in the starlight. "I think your grandfather has searched the library forty times, and I think he knows it is gone. He is waiting for a miracle." A pause. "I have never known you to wait for one."

He opens his mouth, and she holds up a hand.

"I do not want to know. I want you to know that when the day comes that you are ready to tell me, I will be sitting on the other side of the door." She turns toward the house. "Sleep. You have four days."

She goes in. The door closes.

Lin Jian stands alone in the dark yard with the stars very cold overhead, and the gray band aching faintly on his ankle, and the last words of the Hollow's oldest law turning in his head like a wheel.

Before the council, on proof.

He has the proof of the theft. He does not yet have the proof of the thing that matters.

But he has four days. And somewhere in the back of his head, in a place he has not opened since he was three years old, there is a perfect picture of a lacquered tube with a brass cap, drawn to the last strand of ink.

He looks at his hands for a long time.

Then he goes in to bed, and does not sleep.
